title: Week 32 Check-In · Letter to a Future 5th Grader
description: This week you wrote a letter to a future 5th grader about two of the year's novels, studied voice, tone and pacing, read a poem aloud, and did a final review of the year's grammar, roots and spelling.
chapters: The five novels + one real Gold Rush letter

questions.label: Agreement
questions.text: Which sentence is ready to publish?
options: Each of the boys were changed by the journey.
Each of the boys was changed by the journey.
each of the boys was changed by the journey.
Each of the boys was changed by the journey
questions.from: 32.4 Grammar (One Last Check); 32.3 Grammar (was / were); 32.1 Grammar sort
questions.status: replaced (was a 'which sentence has the best voice' item with three options and no grammar rule)

questions.label: Titles
questions.text: Which sentence capitalizes the book title correctly?
options: I read carry on, mr. bowditch in the fall.
I read Carry On, Mr. Bowditch in the fall.
I read Carry on, mr. Bowditch in the fall.
I read Carry On Mr Bowditch in the fall.

questions.label: Fix a Run-On
questions.text: Fix the capitals and the run-on. Write the sentences correctly.
questions.excerpt: i chose this book because it made me laugh it also made me think about keeping promises
questions.key: I chose this book because it made me laugh. It also made me think about keeping promises. (Or: ...laugh, and it also made me think... Capital I twice; the run-on split or joined correctly; end mark.)
questions.from: 32.1-32.4 Daily Oral Language; 32.4 Grammar (before and after)
questions.status: fixed (same skill; a shorter sentence with no book claims)

questions.text: In the word inaudible, what does in- mean?
questions.from: 32.4 Morphology (Which word part is doing the work?); 32.3 build the word

questions.label: Root
questions.text: The root port means carry. Which word is built from it?
questions.from: 32.3 word game; year-long root review (port, Bowditch unit)

options: strength to keep going through hard times

questions.from: 32.1 tap the correct spellings; 32.4 Spelling (type the right spelling)

questions.key: I receive a new book every week, and I separate the ones I love from the ones that embarrass me. (receive, separate, embarrass)

questions.label: Word Families
questions.text: Which word belongs to the same word family as persist?

questions.label: Pacing
questions.text: Read the lines from By the Great Horn Spoon!, Chapter 18. Why does Sid Fleischman use three short sentences?
questions.excerpt: They looked very much like a family. They felt like a family. They were a family.
options: Each sentence goes one step further, and the short last one lands hardest.
He forgot to join them with commas.
Short sentences always mean a chapter is ending.

questions.label: Tone
questions.text: Captain Prince doubted Nat's figures, and Nat turned out to be right. What is Nat's tone in these lines from Carry On, Mr. Bowditch, Chapter 12?
questions.excerpt: “Of course,” Nat said. “It’s a simple matter of mathematics, sir.”
questions.from: 32.3 Read Like a Writer (tone); 32.3 Virtue Watch

questions.label: Primary Source
questions.text: Louise Clappe wrote letters from a California mining camp in 1851 and 1852. Why is her letter a primary source?
options: She wrote it at the time, about a place she was living in.
It is a novel about the Gold Rush.
Optima wrote it for this lesson.
questions.from: 32.2 card 'Real history: letters that crossed time'; week 31 sources

questions.label: Poetry
questions.text: In Amy Lowell’s “Wind and Silver,” the third line is much longer than the others. How should a reader read it aloud?
options: Let it run a little faster, like the flashing fish-ponds, then land softly on the last line.
Skip it, because it is too long.
Read it the same way as every other line.
questions.from: 32.2 Poetry Corner (read it three ways; the tip); 32.4 Poetry Corner

questions.label: Your Letter
questions.text: Write the claim sentence of your letter (Read ___ before ___). Then write one reason, with a moment from each of the two books.
questions.key: A claim that names two of the five novels; one reason; a real moment (or exact words) from each book that supports it.
